strengths: Substantial and impactful dataset contribution: UniEM-3M provides 5,091 high-resolution electron micrographs with nearly 3 million instance-level segmentation masks and 9-attribute structured descriptions, addressing a major data scarcity bottleneck in automated materials characterization.

Well-engineered annotation and curation pipeline: The authors developed a specialized web-based platform tailored for extreme instance densities (often hundreds to thousands of instances per image) with human-in-the-loop verification, cross-VLM attribute annotation, and expert materials scientist auditing.

Comprehensive benchmark and analysis: The paper evaluates diverse instance segmentation paradigms (anchor-based, anchor-free, and 2D vector field-based), convincingly demonstrating why flow-based representations are substantially more robust for crowded microstructural instances compared to standard natural image baselines.

Thorough exploration of generative modeling: Fine-tuning SDXL with structured textual attributes and LoRA demonstrates meaningful utility for compositional data augmentation, distribution matching, and pre-training (improving downstream segmentation performance across varying training set sizes).
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding public release scope: The manuscript mentions in the Abstract and Section 1 that only 'a subset of which will be made publicly available' and that the diffusion model serves as a privacy surrogate. For a dataset/benchmark contribution, withholding a substantial fraction of the benchmark data limits full reproducibility and community utility; the authors should clearly specify the proportion and composition of the publicly released subset.

Limited architectural novelty in UniEM-Net: While UniEM-Net serves as a strong, solid baseline, it largely combines established ideas from Cellpose (energy function and 2D gradient field tracking) and CellViT with a SAM-ViT backbone. The algorithmic novelty is relatively modest.

Unclear mask generation protocol for synthetic training: In Section 5.1 (Table 3 and Figure 6), models are trained/pretrained on up to 30K generated images. It is not fully articulated in the text how the corresponding instance segmentation masks were obtained for these purely synthetic images (e.g., via model pseudo-labeling, joint generation, or unsupervised pre-training).

strengths: Significance and scale of annotation: Microstructural characterization in materials science lacks large-scale, densely annotated instance-level datasets. Providing 5,091 raw electron micrographs with nearly 3 million instance annotations represents a massive human-in-the-loop annotation and curation effort.

Comprehensive benchmark of diverse paradigms: The paper evaluates a wide spectrum of instance segmentation architectures (anchor-based like Mask R-CNN/HTC, anchor-free query/contour-based like Mask2Former/StarDist, and 2D vector field-based methods like CellViT/Cellpose). This clearly highlights where natural image architectures fail in ultra-dense, non-semantic microstructural regimes.

Integration of structured multimodal descriptions: Annotating micrographs with 9 decoupled categorical/descriptive dimensions (morphology, density, layering, distribution, etc.) via multi-VLM cross-checking and expert validation adds valuable structure for conditional generation and potential vision-language tasks.

Empirical validation of generative data: The fine-tuned SDXL model is thoroughly evaluated not only via standard generation metrics (FID, style similarity) but also through downstream utility experiments, showing that synthetic data can serve as an effective pre-training and data augmentation source.
weaknesses: Benchmarking integrity undermined by partial dataset release: The abstract and introduction explicitly state that only a 'subset' of UniEM-3M will be made publicly available, suggesting the generative diffusion model act as a proxy. For a submission whose primary contribution is a benchmark and dataset, withholding the full ground-truth test and training splits prevents the community from directly reproducing the benchmark results in Table 2 or training competitive models on the full distribution.

Limited methodological novelty in UniEM-Net: UniEM-Net appears to be an adaptation of the Cellpose / CellViT formulation (predicting 2D spatial gradient/flow vectors pointing to instance centers combined with foreground probability maps) swapped onto a SAM-ViT backbone. The core modeling pipeline introduces limited algorithmic novelty beyond existing bio-imaging flow baselines.

Inconsistent benchmark training and evaluation protocol: In Table 2, anchor-based methods are trained and evaluated solely on the sparse subset due to memory/proposal limits, whereas 2D-field methods are trained and evaluated across splits. The exact train/val/test counts for the sparse vs. dense partitions are not clearly detailed in the main text, making direct comparisons difficult.

Absence of materials-specific scientific evaluation: While standard computer vision metrics (mAP@0.5 and PQ@0.5) are reported, electron micrographs are ultimately segmented to extract physical parameters (e.g., grain size distributions, aspect ratios, porosity fractions, or nearest-neighbor distances). Validating whether the segmentation errors lead to statistically significant distortions in derived metallurgical/materials properties would substantially elevate the scientific impact.

strengths: Substantial and impactful dataset contribution: UniEM-3M provides 5,091 high-resolution electron micrographs across diverse material systems and imaging modalities with nearly 3 million instance masks, addressing an acute lack of large-scale, high-density instance-level benchmarks in materials science.

Rigorously designed data curation and annotation pipeline: The multi-stage annotation framework—combining automated text removal, VLM-based cross-verified structured descriptions (Gemini and GPT), custom web-based annotation tools with edge-snapping, and human-in-the-loop curriculum pseudo-labeling—is well-engineered and practical for handling extreme instance densities (>2,000 instances/image).

Effective integration of generative modeling: Fine-tuning SDXL with LoRA using decoupled structured attribute prompts provides controllable synthesis and data augmentation. Experiments in Section 5 empirically demonstrate that pretraining or augmenting with synthetic micrographs leads to tangible performance gains in downstream segmentation.

Comprehensive benchmark analysis: The paper benchmarks a broad range of instance segmentation paradigms (anchor-based, anchor-free, and 2D field-based methods), clearly illustrating that standard natural-image architectures break down under extreme microstructural crowding, whereas flow-based formulations (e.g., UniEM-Net, Cellpose) are markedly superior.
weaknesses: Ambiguity and limitation regarding public release: The manuscript explicitly notes that only 'a subset of which will be made publicly available'. For a dataset and benchmark paper, withholding portions of the dataset hampers full reproducibility and community-wide benchmarking. The authors should clarify the exact size, licensing, and criteria of the public release compared to the full 5,091 images.

Limited architectural novelty of UniEM-Net: While UniEM-Net performs well, its technical formulation is essentially an adaptation of the Cellpose vector-field framework paired with a SAM-ViT backbone. The algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental.

Incomplete benchmarking across subsets: In Table 2, several mainstream baselines (Mask R-CNN, HTC, YOLACT, Mask2Former) are omitted from the 'Dense' subset evaluation (marked as '-'). While the authors mention proposal/NMS memory bottlenecks, providing patch-based evaluation or reporting their failure/out-of-memory modes quantitatively would offer a more rigorous comparison.

Unclear mask generation procedure for synthetic data: Table 3 evaluates training on up to 30K generated images ('Gen'). It is not entirely clear whether these 30K synthetic samples were paired with synthetic masks via joint generation, pseudo-labeled by an interim segmentation model, or used strictly for self-supervised/representation pre-training as hinted in Section 5.1.

strengths: High-impact dataset for materials science and scientific computer vision: EM3M addresses a prominent data scarcity bottleneck by providing 5,091 curated electron micrographs accompanied by nearly 3 million fine-grained instance segmentation masks and structured multi-attribute text annotations.

Rigor in annotation and quality control: The multi-stage annotation process (human expert seed set, pseudo-labeling, peer review, and expert audit) is well-designed. The paper supports this with quantitative validation, reporting inter-annotator agreement and Krippendorff's Alpha across pipeline stages.

Comprehensive benchmark highlighting real-world CV bottlenecks: Benchmarking across two-stage, one-stage, query-based, and bottom-up paradigms provides valuable empirical insights. It convincingly demonstrates how standard natural-image architectures (e.g., Mask2Former, Mask DINO) break down under extreme instance densities and memory bounds, whereas bottom-up flow-based representations excel.

Effective integration of generative modeling: Using fine-tuned SDXL conditioned on structured attribute templates proves to be a practical and impactful data engine. The synthetic data is thoroughly evaluated both distributionally (FID, DINO style similarity) and functionally through segmentation pre-training and data augmentation ablations.

Strong and well-engineered baseline: The proposed UniAIMS baseline thoughtfully adapts Cellpose to handle extreme intra-image scale variations and large-scale multi-GPU training via Large Scale Jittering (LSJ), CUDA-accelerated flow computation, and a ViT-B backbone, significantly outperforming prior baselines.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol asymmetry across architectures: Detection- and query-based models are benchmarked exclusively on the sparse subset (<100 instances), while bottom-up methods are evaluated on the full dataset. While the paper justifies this via default framework limits and memory bottlenecks during training, evaluating standard architectures using sliding-window / patch-based inference or increasing max detection / query limits would have provided a more rigorous comparison on the dense sets.

Under-explored vision-language benchmark: Although the dataset features structured 9-attribute textual descriptions and the authors emphasize multimodal understanding, the experimental benchmarking focuses predominantly on instance segmentation and image generation. Benchmarking downstream multimodal tasks (e.g., microstructural attribute prediction, captioning, or visual question answering) would have strengthened the multimodal claims.

Modest architectural novelty: UniAIMS is primarily an engineering adaptation and optimization of existing frameworks (Cellpose, LSJ, modern ViT backbones) rather than a novel conceptual segmentation paradigm. While fitting for a Dataset/Benchmark contribution, the algorithmic novelty remains incremental.

strengths: Significance and scale of the dataset: Microstructural characterization in materials science has long been constrained by small-scale or classification-only datasets. EM3M contributes 5,091 experimental electron micrographs with nearly 3 million instance segmentation masks across SEM and TEM, addressing a critical data bottleneck in scientific computer vision.

Structured multimodal annotations: The curation of 9 disentangled attribute dimensions (morphology, density, layering, texture, etc.) via a multi-LLM cross-validation and domain-expert review pipeline provides high-quality structured metadata that bridges visual microstructures with textual semantic concepts.

Rigorous quality control and validation: The authors evaluate inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha and Panoptic Quality) across data curation stages (Table 2), explicitly measuring the mitigation of pseudo-labeling bias and ensuring annotation reliability.

Thorough benchmarking across paradigms: The paper systematically evaluates two-stage, one-stage, query-based, and bottom-up/proxy-based instance segmentation architectures, highlighting the distinct failure modes and hardware bottlenecks (e.g., peak memory consumption and query limits) of detection-based/transformer methods in dense scenes.

Actionable baseline and generative pipeline: The proposed UniAIMS adapts the flow-based Cellpose framework for multi-GPU distributed training and high intra-image scale variance (via LSJ), delivering strong segmentation results. Furthermore, the fine-tuned SDXL data engine is validated both distributionally and by demonstrating measurable downstream segmentation gains.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in UniAIMS: As acknowledged by the authors, UniAIMS primarily consists of practical implementation and engineering adaptations of Cellpose (LSJ data augmentation, removal of the size model, ViT backbone, and CUDA-accelerated flow computation) rather than a novel segmentation methodology.

Asymmetric benchmarking between paradigms: Detection-based and query-based architectures are only evaluated on the sparse subset (<100 instances/image) due to MMDetection default limitations and memory constraints. While the hardware bottleneck analysis in Sec. 14.2 is insightful, evaluating patch-based/tiled inference or adjusting proposal/query limits would provide a fairer and more comprehensive comparison on the full dataset.

Limited multimodal evaluation beyond text-to-image generation: Although structured textual descriptions are a major component of EM3M, they are primarily utilized for text-to-image conditioning. The manuscript does not benchmark multimodal understanding tasks (e.g., micrograph captioning, visual question answering, or attribute prediction/retrieval), leaving the vision-language utility partly unexplored.

Domain-specific physical validation: While generative quality is evaluated via FID and DINO cosine similarity, the synthetic micrographs are not evaluated for domain-specific physical or crystallographic correctness, which is critical for real-world material diagnostics.

strengths: Substantial and timely dataset contribution: EM3M provides 5,091 high-resolution electron micrographs with nearly 3 million instance masks, vastly exceeding prior public datasets in materials science in both scale and instance density (frequently exceeding 500-2,000 instances per image).

Rigorous curation and annotation methodology: The multi-stage human-in-the-loop pipeline combines model-assisted pseudo-labeling with custom annotation tools (e.g., magnetic lasso with Sobel snapping), expert peer review, and quantitative inter-annotator validation (KA = 0.818, PQ = 0.784), ensuring high annotation quality.

Well-structured multimodal attributes: Sourcing 9 disentangled scientific and visual dimensions via LLM cross-verification and expert correction provides rich metadata suitable for multimodal reasoning and controllable generation.

Comprehensive benchmarking across paradigms: The paper thoroughly benchmarks 12 representative instance segmentation algorithms across two-stage, one-stage, query-based, and bottom-up paradigms, providing insightful evidence on where standard natural-image architectures fail in ultra-dense, texture-heavy scientific scenes.

Solid baseline engineering (UniAIMS): Adapting the Cellpose flow-based framework with Large Scale Jittering (LSJ), ViT backbones, distributed multi-GPU training, and custom CUDA acceleration creates an effective, scalable baseline.

Demonstrated utility of generative augmentation: Fine-tuning SDXL using structured text prompts is quantitatively evaluated (FID, DINO style similarity) and shown to boost downstream segmentation performance when combined with real data.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol disparity: Detection- and query-based architectures are evaluated only on the 'sparse' subset (<100 instances per image), whereas bottom-up models are evaluated on both sparse and full sets. While memory and architectural constraints in MMDetection are acknowledged, exploring standard dense-object strategies (such as sliding-window tiling or increasing max detections) would have made the comparison more exhaustive.

Reliance on lenient metrics: The main quantitative benchmark only reports mAP@0.5 and PQ@0.5. As the authors frankly note in the Open Problems section, UniAIMS drops from 0.704 PQ@50 to 0.340 PQ@90. Reporting AP@[0.5:0.95] across all methods in Table 3 would provide a much clearer picture of boundary delineation fidelity.

Domain-specific physical validation of generated samples: While FID and feature-based style scores are evaluated, quantitative domain validation (e.g., measuring statistical alignment of grain size distributions or circularity between real and generated samples) is missing.

Class-agnostic focus: The dataset and benchmark treat segmentation primarily as class-agnostic particle/grain extraction. Real-world materials characterization often requires distinguishing multiple concurrent phases or distinguishing matrix from precipitates, which is not explored in the current benchmark formulation.
